Proper fiducial mark placement, pad design, component arrangement, and panelization can help reduce potential problems during solder paste printing, SMT placement, and reflow soldering. PCB designers should therefore take actual manufacturing processes into account from the early design stage. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement by: Mila Oct 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout is not an arbitrary process. It must follow certain design rules to ensure electrical performance, thermal management, and assembly quality. In addition to general layout requirements, some components have specific placement constraints that must be considered during PCB component placement. 1. Placement Requirements for Press-Fit Components For right-angle male and female press-fit components, no components taller than 3 mm should be placed within 3 mm of the component, and no soldered components should be placed within 1.5 mm. On the opposite side of the PCB, no components should be placed within 2.5 mm of the center of the press-fit pin holes. For straight male and female press-fit components, no components should be placed within 1 mm of the component. If a protective sleeve is required on the opposite side of the PCB, no components should be placed within 1 mm of the sleeve edge. If no sleeve is installed, no components should be placed within 2.5 mm of the press-fit holes. For hot-plug sockets used with grounding connectors in European-style connectors, components should not be placed within 6.5 mm of the front end of long pins or within 2.0 mm of the front end of short pins. For long pins on 2 mm FB single-pin power connectors, no components should be placed within 8 mm in front of the corresponding board-mounted socket. （Press-Fit Connector Placement and Clearance Requirements） 2. Placement Requirements for Temperature-Sensitive Components During PCB component placement, temperature-sensitive components should be kept away from high-heat components whenever possible. For example, electrolytic capacitors should be protected from prolonged exposure to excessive temperatures, while crystal oscillators require attention to temperature variations that may affect frequency stability. Components used for temperature sensing should be placed according to the target being measured and the actual heat-transfer path. They should be positioned to accurately reflect the target temperature while minimizing the influence of other heat-generating components, which could otherwise cause measurement errors or false triggering. Heat-generating components that can withstand high temperatures should be placed in locations that support effective heat dissipation, taking the actual airflow path into account. Components with limited heat resistance should be kept away from high-temperature areas. Where possible, avoid placing them directly in the airflow path downstream of other heat-generating components or where they may affect temperature-sensitive components. （PCB Layout for Thermal-Sensitive Components） 3. Placement Requirements for Polarized Components Through-hole devices (THD) with polarity or directional requirements should be oriented consistently and arranged neatly to facilitate insertion, soldering, and visual inspection. Surface-mount components (SMC) with polarity should preferably have a consistent orientation, provided that electrical connections and routing requirements are met. Components of the same type should be arranged neatly to simplify assembly and inspection. Common polarized components include electrolytic capacitors, tantalum capacitors, and diodes. During PCB layout, always verify component polarity markings against the schematic and PCB footprint to prevent circuit malfunctions caused by incorrect orientation. （Polarized Component Orientation in PCB Layout） 4. Placement Requirements for Through-Hole Reflow Components For PCBs with a dimension greater than 300 mm along the non-conveying edge, the placement of heavier components should be planned carefully, taking into account board thickness, support conditions, and component weight. Where appropriate, avoid placing heavy components in the center of the board to reduce the risk of PCB deformation and interference with component insertion or previously placed components. To facilitate component insertion, components may be placed closer to the insertion operation side, depending on the actual assembly process and equipment requirements. For long components, such as memory module sockets, the component's longitudinal axis should preferably be parallel to the PCB conveying direction, subject to the requirements of the production equipment and assembly process. Verify Now Blog > PCB Routing Guidelines for Ground, Power, and Signal Traces PCB Routing Guidelines for Ground, Power, and Signal Traces by: Mila Oct 22,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB routing PCB routing guidelines PCB trace routing PCB ground plane PCB signal integrity Poor PCB routing can lead to signal integrity issues, EMC failures, and power instability, even when component selection and schematic design are correct. These problems often stem from discontinuous return paths, improper trace routing, or insufficient consideration of electrical constraints. This article covers key PCB routing guidelines for ground planes, critical signals, and power traces, along with a practical routing workflow and common mistakes to help engineers improve design reliability and manufacturability. Understanding PCB Routing Priorities PCB routing should not follow a rigid sequence of routing signals first, power traces second, and ground connections last. For multilayer boards, the stackup and reference planes should be planned before routing begins. High-speed interfaces, sensitive analog circuits, and switching power supplies also require early consideration of critical signal paths and current return paths. In practice, the following approach provides a useful starting point. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and grounding strategy. Determine which layers will serve as reference planes, provide continuous reference paths for critical nets wherever possible, and establish a grounding strategy appropriate for the circuit. Step 2: Route critical nets first. These include high-speed differential signals, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and switching power supply loops with strict current-loop requirements. Such nets often have tighter constraints on routing length, return paths, impedance, or noise coupling. Step 3: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths, copper areas, and routing paths based on operating current, allowable voltage drop, temperature rise, and power integrity requirements. Step 4: Complete ordinary low-speed signal routing. Route signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O (GPIO) using the remaining routing space while meeting electrical and manufacturing requirements. This is a general guideline rather than a fixed sequence for every PCB. Routing priorities should be adjusted according to circuit topology, component placement, signal edge rates, power levels, and design constraints. For multilayer boards, planning continuous reference planes in advance is generally more important than simply routing all ground connections first. PCB Ground Plane and Return Path Design A ground plane provides a reference for signals and a return path for power and signal currents. Poor ground plane design can increase return-path inductance and loop area, potentially affecting signal integrity, power integrity, and EMC performance. Key Ground Plane Design Principles Prioritize reference plane continuity. For multilayer PCBs, a continuous ground plane should be used as the reference plane for high-speed and sensitive signals wherever possible. Avoid unnecessary ground plane cuts or slots beneath critical traces. Otherwise, return currents may be forced to detour, increasing loop area and the risk of electromagnetic radiation. Choose a grounding strategy based on the circuit. Digital, analog, and power circuits may have different noise and return-current requirements. However, physically separating DGND, AGND, and PGND and connecting them at a single point is not a universal requirement. In many mixed-signal designs, a continuous ground plane combined with careful component placement and current-path management can provide better noise performance. If separate ground regions or single-point connections are necessary, determine the connection strategy based on circuit topology and the component manufacturer's recommendations. Keep critical ground connections short. The ground terminals of decoupling capacitors, return terminals of power devices, and ground connections near interfaces should use low-inductance paths whenever possible. Properly placed ground vias can help reduce parasitic inductance. The number and placement of vias in high-frequency regions should be determined according to current paths, stackup structure, and EMC requirements. Common Ground Plane Design Mistakes For multilayer PCBs, using a continuous ground plane is generally preferable to relying on numerous narrow, manually routed ground traces. For single-layer and double-layer boards, copper pours, trace routing, and component placement should be coordinated to provide continuous, low-impedance return paths for critical nets wherever possible. Common mistakes include: Splitting the ground plane unnecessarily and forcing return currents to take longer paths. Routing critical high-speed signals across ground plane splits or slots. Placing decoupling capacitors too far from power pins or using long ground connections. Leaving unnecessary floating copper areas that introduce parasitic effects. Connecting different ground nets without a clear circuit-level justification. There is no single ground trace width that applies to every PCB. Ground traces carrying significant current should be sized according to current, copper thickness, allowable temperature rise, and voltage drop. For multilayer boards, a ground plane will often provide lower return-path impedance than narrow, manually routed ground traces. Common Failure Analysis Consider an industrial data acquisition board where ordinary signals were routed before the grounding arrangement was fully considered. Several traces fragmented the reference plane in the analog section, affecting the return paths of some sampling signals. During operation, the board exhibited fluctuating measurements and failed to meet the expected EMC performance. Troubleshooting should focus on ground plane continuity, signal return paths, analog and digital component placement, and power supply noise coupling rather than assuming that the routing sequence alone caused the failure. Corrective actions should address the actual failure mechanism and may include rerouting traces, restoring reference plane continuity, or optimizing component placement. Routing Critical Signals and Power Traces High-speed signals, sensitive analog signals, and power circuits have different design constraints. They should be routed according to their electrical characteristics rather than assigned priorities based solely on signal frequency or trace width. High-Speed Signals and Sensitive Analog Signals High-speed differential pairs , clock signals, DDR signals, RF signals, and sensitive analog nets such as ADC inputs often require their routing paths to be considered during the component placement stage. （High-Speed PCB Routing and Differential Pair Design） Control routing length and return paths. Critical nets should avoid unnecessary detours and vias while maintaining a continuous reference plane. Whether a high-speed trace is sufficiently short depends on factors such as signal rise time, propagation delay, and circuit requirements, not just clock frequency. Control impedance and timing. For high-speed interfaces such as USB and HDMI, target impedance, trace width, spacing, and other routing constraints should be determined according to interface specifications and the actual PCB stackup. Differential impedance cannot be determined by trace width alone; dielectric thickness, copper thickness, reference planes, and trace geometry also affect it. For DDR and other timing-sensitive parallel interfaces, length matching should follow the timing budget specified by the component manufacturer rather than applying the same length-matching requirement to every signal. Reduce crosstalk risk. The 3W rule can serve as an initial trace spacing guideline, but it does not guarantee that crosstalk will be eliminated. Actual spacing requirements also depend on parallel routing length, dielectric thickness, signal edge rate, and stackup structure. Signal integrity simulation or testing may be necessary for critical nets. Keep signals away from major noise sources. Sensitive analog traces should be routed away from switching nodes, high-current loops, and other noisy areas whenever possible. For high-speed signals, the need for additional clearance from the board edge or the use of ground via fences should be evaluated according to specific EMC requirements. Ordinary Low-Speed Signal Routing Signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O typically do not require the same level of impedance control as high-speed interfaces. However, they must still meet electrical and reliability requirements. During routing: Meet minimum trace width, spacing, and manufacturing requirements. Avoid unnecessary detours and densely packed parallel traces. Keep traces away from critical high-speed nets, sensitive analog areas, and high-current power loops. Evaluate crosstalk and EMC risks for low-speed interfaces with fast edge rates or connections to external cables. Ordinary low-speed signals can generally be routed more flexibly, but they should not be treated as nets that only need electrical connectivity. Power Traces and Power Loops Power routing must provide sufficient current-carrying capacity, control voltage drop and temperature rise, and maintain appropriate current paths for critical power circuits. Size traces according to actual requirements. Trace width should be determined by copper thickness, whether the trace is on an outer or inner layer, operating current, allowable temperature rise, and trace length. High-current nets also require evaluation of copper temperature rise, voltage drop, and current density at connection points. A fixed trace-width-to-current table alone is not sufficient to determine whether a design is safe. Minimize critical power loop areas. For switching regulators such as DC-DC converters, prioritize the layout of high-(di/dt) current loops. Keep relevant connections short and follow the IC manufacturer's recommended layout for input bypass capacitors, power devices, and other critical components. This helps reduce parasitic inductance and noise radiation. Control noise coupling. Switching nodes and high-current loops should be kept away from sensitive analog signals and other noise-sensitive nets whenever possible. Spacing between different power rails should be determined by voltage, current, switching noise, and insulation requirements rather than by a blanket rule that all power traces at different voltage levels must be separated. Use decoupling capacitors appropriately. Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to their corresponding power pins and connected to the power and reference planes through low-inductance paths. Capacitance, package size, and capacitor combinations should be selected according to component requirements and power integrity targets. Decoupling capacitors cannot compensate for poor power loop design. Power traces are not always better when made wider. Excessive trace width can consume routing space needed by critical nets. Similarly, inner-layer copper is not inherently worse than outer-layer routing for heat dissipation. The appropriate routing approach depends on current capacity, copper area, heat transfer paths, and stackup structure. A Practical PCB Routing Workflow After the stackup and component placement have been planned, the following workflow provides a useful starting point. The sequence should be adjusted to suit the constraints of each project. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and board outline. Define the board outline, keep-out areas, connector positions, and layer functions. Establish the reference planes and grounding strategy for critical nets. Step 2: Complete critical component placement. Position high-speed interface ICs, crystals, ADCs, power ICs, and power devices with consideration for signal paths, power loops, thermal performance, and EMC requirements. Step 3: Route critical nets. Prioritize nets with strict timing, impedance, noise, or return-path constraints. These may include high-speed differential pairs, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and critical switching power loops. Step 4: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths and routing paths according to current, voltage drop, and temperature rise requirements. Check decoupling capacitor placement and power return paths. Step 5: Complete ordinary signal routing. Route GPIO, buttons, indicator LEDs, and other general-purpose nets while meeting design rules and avoiding unnecessary interference with critical nets. Step 6: Review copper pours and grounding connections. Complete ground pours, check thermal relief connections and ground vias, verify reference plane continuity, and remove unnecessary floating copper. Ensure that copper pours do not compromise return paths for critical nets. Step 7: Run DRC and perform a design review. Check trace width, spacing, vias, impedance constraints, differential pairs, length matching, and manufacturability. For high-speed or high-power designs, perform signal integrity analysis, power integrity analysis, thermal analysis, or EMC validation as appropriate. Common PCB Routing Problems and How to Avoid Them Common Failure 1: Discontinuous Reference Planes Cause EMC Problems On a controller board, high-speed signals were routed across a split in the reference plane to avoid other nets. This increased the distance that return currents had to travel, and high-frequency radiation problems appeared during testing. Such failures should be investigated by examining the routing, reference planes, and test results. Possible corrective actions include rerouting the signals, restoring reference plane continuity, or rearranging components and other nets to reduce return-path discontinuities. Common Failure 2: Digital Noise Interferes with Sensitive Analog Signals An ADC circuit exhibited fluctuating readings. Investigation revealed that the analog input traces were routed close to digital signals and a switching power supply, creating potential noise coupling paths. Optimization should focus on the analog input routing, reference plane, front-end filtering, component placement, and power supply noise. Measurements should be used to confirm the dominant interference source. Only after identifying the failure mechanism should engineers adjust trace spacing, grounding, or filtering. （Common PCB Routing Mistakes and Design Rule Violations） Conclusion Effective PCB routing requires more than electrical connectivity and compliance with design rules. It also involves careful consideration of reference planes, return paths, signal integrity, power integrity, current-carrying capacity, and electromagnetic compatibility. Planning the stackup and critical nets in advance, applying routing strategies appropriate to each circuit, and performing a thorough design review can help reduce design defects, lower rework costs, and improve product reliability. Common Failure Analysis Consider an industrial data acquisition board where ordinary signals were routed before the grounding arrangement was fully considered. Several traces fragmented the reference plane in the analog section, affecting the return paths of some sampling signals. During operation, the board exhibited fluctuating measurements and failed to meet the expected EMC performance. Troubleshooting should focus on ground plane continuity, signal return paths, analog and digital component placement, and power supply noise coupling rather than assuming that the routing sequence alone caused the failure. Corrective actions should address the actual failure mechanism and may include rerouting traces, restoring reference plane continuity, or optimizing component placement. Routing Critical Signals and Power Traces High-speed signals, sensitive analog signals, and power circuits have different design constraints. They should be routed according to their electrical characteristics rather than assigned priorities based solely on signal frequency or trace width. High-Speed Signals and Sensitive Analog Signals High-speed differential pairs , clock signals, DDR signals, RF signals, and sensitive analog nets such as ADC inputs often require their routing paths to be considered during the component placement stage. （High-Speed PCB Routing and Differential Pair Design） Control routing length and return paths. Critical nets should avoid unnecessary detours and vias while maintaining a continuous reference plane. Whether a high-speed trace is sufficiently short depends on factors such as signal rise time, propagation delay, and circuit requirements, not just clock frequency. Control impedance and timing. For high-speed interfaces such as USB and HDMI, target impedance, trace width, spacing, and other routing constraints should be determined according to interface specifications and the actual PCB stackup. Differential impedance cannot be determined by trace width alone; dielectric thickness, copper thickness, reference planes, and trace geometry also affect it. For DDR and other timing-sensitive parallel interfaces, length matching should follow the timing budget specified by the component manufacturer rather than applying the same length-matching requirement to every signal. Reduce crosstalk risk. The 3W rule can serve as an initial trace spacing guideline, but it does not guarantee that crosstalk will be eliminated. Actual spacing requirements also depend on parallel routing length, dielectric thickness, signal edge rate, and stackup structure. Signal integrity simulation or testing may be necessary for critical nets. Keep signals away from major noise sources. Sensitive analog traces should be routed away from switching nodes, high-current loops, and other noisy areas whenever possible. For high-speed signals, the need for additional clearance from the board edge or the use of ground via fences should be evaluated according to specific EMC requirements. Ordinary Low-Speed Signal Routing Signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O typically do not require the same level of impedance control as high-speed interfaces. However, they must still meet electrical and reliability requirements. During routing: Meet minimum trace width, spacing, and manufacturing requirements. Avoid unnecessary detours and densely packed parallel traces. Keep traces away from critical high-speed nets, sensitive analog areas, and high-current power loops. Evaluate crosstalk and EMC risks for low-speed interfaces with fast edge rates or connections to external cables. Ordinary low-speed signals can generally be routed more flexibly, but they should not be treated as nets that only need electrical connectivity. Power Traces and Power Loops Power routing must provide sufficient current-carrying capacity, control voltage drop and temperature rise, and maintain appropriate current paths for critical power circuits. Size traces according to actual requirements. Trace width should be determined by copper thickness, whether the trace is on an outer or inner layer, operating current, allowable temperature rise, and trace length. High-current nets also require evaluation of copper temperature rise, voltage drop, and current density at connection points. A fixed trace-width-to-current table alone is not sufficient to determine whether a design is safe. Minimize critical power loop areas. For switching regulators such as DC-DC converters, prioritize the layout of high-(di/dt) current loops. Keep relevant connections short and follow the IC manufacturer's recommended layout for input bypass capacitors, power devices, and other critical components. This helps reduce parasitic inductance and noise radiation. Control noise coupling. Switching nodes and high-current loops should be kept away from sensitive analog signals and other noise-sensitive nets whenever possible. Spacing between different power rails should be determined by voltage, current, switching noise, and insulation requirements rather than by a blanket rule that all power traces at different voltage levels must be separated. Use decoupling capacitors appropriately. Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to their corresponding power pins and connected to the power and reference planes through low-inductance paths. Capacitance, package size, and capacitor combinations should be selected according to component requirements and power integrity targets. Decoupling capacitors cannot compensate for poor power loop design. Power traces are not always better when made wider. Excessive trace width can consume routing space needed by critical nets. Similarly, inner-layer copper is not inherently worse than outer-layer routing for heat dissipation. The appropriate routing approach depends on current capacity, copper area, heat transfer paths, and stackup structure. A Practical PCB Routing Workflow After the stackup and component placement have been planned, the following workflow provides a useful starting point. The sequence should be adjusted to suit the constraints of each project. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and board outline. Define the board outline, keep-out areas, connector positions, and layer functions. Establish the reference planes and grounding strategy for critical nets. Step 2: Complete critical component placement. Position high-speed interface ICs, crystals, ADCs, power ICs, and power devices with consideration for signal paths, power loops, thermal performance, and EMC requirements. Step 3: Route critical nets. Prioritize nets with strict timing, impedance, noise, or return-path constraints. These may include high-speed differential pairs, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and critical switching power loops. Step 4: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths and routing paths according to current, voltage drop, and temperature rise requirements. Check decoupling capacitor placement and power return paths. Step 5: Complete ordinary signal routing. Route GPIO, buttons, indicator LEDs, and other general-purpose nets while meeting design rules and avoiding unnecessary interference with critical nets. Step 6: Review copper pours and grounding connections. Complete ground pours, check thermal relief connections and ground vias, verify reference plane continuity, and remove unnecessary floating copper. Ensure that copper pours do not compromise return paths for critical nets. Step 7: Run DRC and perform a design review. Check trace width, spacing, vias, impedance constraints, differential pairs, length matching, and manufacturability. For high-speed or high-power designs, perform signal integrity analysis, power integrity analysis, thermal analysis, or EMC validation as appropriate. Common PCB Routing Problems and How to Avoid Them Common Failure 1: Discontinuous Reference Planes Cause EMC Problems On a controller board, high-speed signals were routed across a split in the reference plane to avoid other nets. This increased the distance that return currents had to travel, and high-frequency radiation problems appeared during testing. Such failures should be investigated by examining the routing, reference planes, and test results. Possible corrective actions include rerouting the signals, restoring reference plane continuity, or rearranging components and other nets to reduce return-path discontinuities. Common Failure 2: Digital Noise Interferes with Sensitive Analog Signals An ADC circuit exhibited fluctuating readings. Investigation revealed that the analog input traces were routed close to digital signals and a switching power supply, creating potential noise coupling paths. Optimization should focus on the analog input routing, reference plane, front-end filtering, component placement, and power supply noise. Measurements should be used to confirm the dominant interference source. Only after identifying the failure mechanism should engineers adjust trace spacing, grounding, or filtering. （Common PCB Routing Mistakes and Design Rule Violations） Conclusion Effective PCB routing requires more than electrical connectivity and compliance with design rules. It also involves careful consideration of reference planes, return paths, signal integrity, power integrity, current-carrying capacity, and electromagnetic compatibility. Planning the stackup and critical nets in advance, applying routing strategies appropriate to each circuit, and performing a thorough design review can help reduce design defects, lower rework costs, and improve product reliability. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. However, pin names alone do not tell the whole story. Always check the IC datasheet to confirm each pin’s function and recommended connections. During PCB layout , pay particular attention to switching nodes, feedback paths, and grounding. Proper component placement and routing can help reduce noise, improve power integrity, and ensure stable operation. Whether you’re designing a simple power supply or a more complex DC-DC converter, understanding these pins is an important step toward reliable PCB design. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly.
